opus-5.5.text:
I think the shift is really about where the bottleneck has moved. For a long time, the hard part of robotics seemed to be the hardware: actuators, joints, sensors, batteries, making something that could physically move reliably without breaking. That work still matters, but over the last few years the hardware has become good enough, and in many cases cheap enough, that it's no longer what's holding us back. You can buy a reasonably capable arm or even a humanoid platform today. What you can't buy is something that knows what to do with it.

So the question becomes intelligence. Can the robot understand the scene in front of it? Can it work out what a person is asking for, break that into steps, and adapt when something unexpected happens, like an object slipping or a door being heavier than expected? That's the brain problem, and it's much harder than it looks, because the physical world is endlessly varied and unforgiving in a way that text or images aren't.

My own background is in vision and generative models, and what we learned there shapes how I see this. Large models showed that if you get the representation right and scale the data, you get surprising generalization. Many of us believe something similar can happen for embodied intelligence. The difference is data. Language models had the internet; robots don't have an internet of physical interaction. So much of the real work in building a robot brain is figuring out where the data comes from: simulation, world models that can imagine outcomes, human videos, teleoperation, and how to combine them so the model actually transfers to real hardware.

There's also a practical reason for the shift. If you build the brain well, it should work across many bodies: different arms, grippers, maybe eventually different form factors entirely. That's a much more scalable position than tying your intelligence to one specific machine. The body becomes more like a peripheral, and the brain becomes the platform.

That said, I don't think brain and body can be fully separated. Intelligence comes from interaction, from the loop between perceiving, acting, and seeing the consequences. A brain that never touches the real world won't truly understand it. So for me, "building the brain" doesn't mean ignoring the body. It means recognizing that the most important open problem now is how a machine learns to understand and act in the physical world, and putting most of our energy there.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the shift comes from a pretty simple observation: the body is not the bottleneck anymore.

If you look at the hardware side, humanoids, dexterous hands, mobile manipulators, the supply chain has matured a lot in the last few years. Motors, sensors, batteries, the cost curve is coming down fast, and there are many companies that can build a decent body. But almost none of those bodies can actually do anything useful in an open environment. You put a robot in a kitchen or a warehouse it has never seen, and it fails. So the hard problem, the thing that determines whether robots become a real industry or stay a demo, is intelligence. It's the brain.

The second reason is what we learned from large language models. Before, every robot task was its own small project: you collect data for this task, train a policy for this task, and it does not transfer. That is a very expensive way to build. What LLMs showed us is that if you scale a general model on enough diverse data, you get capabilities that generalize to things you never explicitly trained for. The whole bet of building a robot brain is that the same thing can happen with embodiment: one model that understands vision, language, and action, and can be deployed across many different bodies.

And that leads to the third point, which is a decoupling of the stack. In computing we went from vertically integrated machines to a world where the operating system and the chips were separate layers, and that is what let the ecosystem explode. I think robotics is going through the same thing. If you build the brain, you do not have to own the body. You can partner with many hardware companies, your data comes from many sources, and your model gets better from all of them. That is a much better flywheel than building one robot end to end.

Of course there are real differences from language. Robot data is scarce, it is expensive to collect, and the physical world does not give you a clean internet-scale corpus. So a lot of the work is actually about data: simulation, video, teleoperation, how to combine them so the model learns physical common sense rather than just memorizing trajectories. But I think the direction is clear. Bodies will become commodities. The brain is where the real value and the real difficulty are.

astra-6.text:
I think it reflects a shift in where people see the main bottleneck. The body gives a robot the ability to move and interact with the world, but the brain determines whether it can do something useful: understand an instruction, recognize the situation, plan an action, and recover when something goes wrong.

You can imagine a robot successfully picking up a cup in a demonstration. The harder question is: can it still do that when the cup moves, the lighting changes, or there’s something blocking its path? That’s the gap between executing a predefined motion and having an ability that generalizes.

But I wouldn’t separate the brain and the body too sharply. A robot’s intelligence has to work through its sensors and physical capabilities. It needs to act, observe the result, and adjust. So, to me, building robot brains means moving toward systems that can learn useful behaviors across tasks and environments, while staying closely connected to the hardware that makes those behaviors possible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it reflects a shift in where the bottleneck is. Building the body is still difficult—you need reliable actuators, sensors, and manufacturing—but a capable body alone doesn’t tell a robot what to do when the situation changes.

The brain has to connect perception, reasoning, and action. If I ask a robot to clear a table, it needs to understand what belongs where, how to grasp different objects, and what to do if something slips. That’s much more than executing a fixed sequence of motions.

So the ambition is to build intelligence that can learn across tasks and, potentially, across different robot bodies. But I wouldn’t separate the two completely. A robot’s intelligence has to be grounded in its physical capabilities. The real test is whether it can act reliably in the world, learn from failure, and handle situations its developers didn’t anticipate.
